transcription: Our fourth participant is Jordan Minor from our Graduate School of Biomedical Science and Engineering. Imagine you've just been diagnosed with early stage press cancer. What are the immediate emotions running through your mind? Scared, stressed, anxious? Now what if I tell you with an 88% chance of living in other 10 years if you do absolutely nothing? Would you seek treatment? Or would you take the risk? This is a problem faced by 20 to 25% of all breast cancer patients, and it's not an easy one to solve. Currently, we have limited methods to detect if an early stage press cancer will progress to more deadly form, or a fatal idol causing no harm for the patient. Most early stage press cancers will never progress to become invasive. However, the thought of living with cancer and all the uncertainties that surround this problem are mental burden for patients. Therefore, the standard of care is typically mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery due to its unpredictability. Initiatives are starting to emerge to combat this problem we know as food for treatment. However, data-driven biomarkers are still desperately needed to separate slow from aggressive cancer. Without these biomarkers, patients may receive treatments such as an optimum balance risk versus outcome. My solution, collagen, collagen is the most abundant fibrous protein in our body, and has recently been identified by other scientists as a biomarker for cancer progression by observing changes in its structural pattern. I want to take this one step further and understand how the cancer cells themselves influence the collagen. Cells interact with collagen through receptors on their cell surface. I hypothesize that by understanding which of these receptors is more active in cancer progression, could lead to development of new biomarkers. To study this, I am using 3D models of human breast cancer cell lines that range from early stage as seen on the left to late stage as seen on the left. All of these cell lines are derived from one patient, allowing the disease progression to be studied under a common genetic background, increasing reliability. I am selectively removing each of these cell surface receptors, and then observing any changes to a cellular invasion as seen here, as well as collagen organization. We've already found that one of these receptors could be a unique biomarker for breast cancer patients. Ultimately, I aim to make the decision of whether to treat or not to treat early stage breast cancer a little easier on patients, improving their life, health, and well-being. Thank you.

title: 3MT_2024_1
transcription: In our final presenter today is Liza White, who is also from the Graduate School of Biomedical Science and Engineering. Imagine that the only water that you have access to is water that smells bad or is dirty looking. Would you want to drink it or cook with it or even clean your house with it without having any knowledge of what is in it or if that could make you sick? Unfortunately that is a reality for over 2 billion people in the world today and this number is expected to increase due to increasing pollution events. But what if this didn't have to be the case? That if our pipelines could be lined with the material that could quickly and accurately tell us one pollution event has occurred. My thesis looks to do just that. I am looking at combining main paper technology and image analysis techniques to create a low cost water monitoring system that could quickly detect one pollution event has occurred. Specifically I am looking at using a diffraction pattern surface that is manufactured in main and how this works is it breaks up light into its component wavelengths. Now you can think of this as how a droplet in the sky breaks up light into its component wavelengths that creates the beautiful rainbows that we all love to look at. Specifically with my work as the water passes over this rainbow film the light is reflected or absorbed in unique ways based on the chemical or biological makeup of the water. We can then image these rainbows and using an image analysis technique we can create data that is similar to water monitoring systems. As of right now we have been able to detect dyes, algae and dust particulates. With the successful completion of my thesis we will have created a low cost solution to be able to quickly and accurately tell someone when the water in their pipelines is contaminated and what it is contaminated with. Thank you. Thank you.

transcription: So I'm very pleased to introduce our first contestant who is Gladys Adou, a Cidua, from the College of Earth, Life and Health Sciences. Imagine a world where every farm is not just a plot of land, but a beacon of Sassina Belaguer culture, where soil health is prioritized, and where every crop is not just thriving, but contributes to the vitality of the land on which they are grown. I grew up in Ghana, where there was struggles of food and nutrition in security. I witnessed the challenges of these communities, and I was motivated by my mother's initiated to grow confused to feed the less fortunate. This decision made me know that I would want to choose a path where I would synthesize ideas to find sustainable solutions to the challenges of these communities and challenges our farmers have faced. In the North, East, our farmers are continuing with short-growing seasons. This poses significant threat to our food systems. In Maine, there is a daunting task on our farmers to protect their soils over the long winter months. In this way, they are limited with time and resources, but there is hope in cover-croping. Cover-crops are just plants that are grown, not for their profits, but for the benefits that they provide to the environment. They help in nutrients retention, controlling erosion, and suppressing weeds. This is why I urge everybody, every farmer, to use cover-crops. However, the challenge is time. This is where interceding comes in. This interceding of farmers can simultaneously grow their cash crops with their cover-crops without negatively impacting the yield of their crops they grow for the market. However, why aren't our farmers incorporating interceding into their farming practices? This is because there is a misconception. Our farmers are of the notion that interceding will create competition, which would negatively affect the quality and the quantity of the crops they are growing for the market. This is where my research comes in. My research dispells this myth. Through my research, I use ecologically-sounding interceding practices to show the farmers that with the right-planted methods, with the correct planting days and selecting the right-cover crop mixes, would not only allow them to increase the vegetables they are growing for the market, but would also create a resilience ecosystem without compromising the quality and the quantity of the crops they are planting. For me, my journey from Ghana to Maine is not just for farming, but it has increased my resilience for research and innovation by collaborating with farmers in local stakeholders. My aim is to create an environment where every agricultural field is a thriving ecosystem, supporting and nurturing both crops and soil health. Thank you.

transcription: Our fifth presenter is Sean Cibli, also from the College of Earth, Life and Health Sciences. Have any of you had a difficult time accessing primary care? Primary care can be delivered by physicians, physician assistants, and more so than ever, nurse practitioners like me, a nurse practitioner, a primary care provider, and a teacher of nurse practitioners. And that's why I'm invested in addressing the lack of access to quality primary care by graduating practice ready family nurse practitioners. It's not using the number of nurse practitioner graduates to address our national shortage of primary care providers, but making sure that they're prepared to care for a population that's more sick. Students are getting very different experiences in their clinical sites, and it might not be sufficient to prepare them for practice. Imagine if you get some scans that look a little suspicious for cancer, and you're working with a nurse practitioner who never had a learning opportunity to practice how to share bad or unexpected news. One promising solution to address these gaps in learning and evaluating students is something called objective structured clinical examinations or ASCII simulations, and I'm just going to call them role plays. This role play teaching activity is used to practice running an appointment with an actor playing the patient in a controlled and a safe setting. The role plays are perfect to experience situations that don't happen very often, but are high stakes. As a doctoral student in nursing education, I explore what students think about these role play experiences through a qualitative study. I did this research with the purpose to improve the role play experience for students into inform nurse practitioner programs how to best implement their role play programs. When I interviewed recent family nurse practitioner graduates, I learned that they really enjoyed the role plays and they thought they were worthwhile. It allowed them to practice the nurse practitioner role, the flow, the words, the technical skills that they then transferred into their clinical learning environments. No participant in my study told me it was like a dress rehearsal. Going through the role play prepared them to step confidently into that role once they were in clinical environments. Some of the routines students developed when they were preparing for and performing their role plays were actually routines that they were still using in their first jobs. And ultimately, students felt that they were better prepared for clinical learning as well as their work because of the role plays and they ultimately wanted more of them. The results of this study helped me make the suggestion to other teachers that following best practice guidelines was really important for students to learn and to be invested in the activity. When you practice ready primary care providers, and nurse practitioners have a proven record of high quality, safe, and cost effective care. And as a teacher, I want to ensure that nurse practitioner graduates are ready for complex patients and my research supports that these oscary role plays can fill gaps and make graduates more prepared to address our health needs, especially in rural areas throughout our state of Maine.

transcription: Our third contestant from the main college of engineering and computing in the Department of Chemical Engineering is Isan Najj Mazar. Hello, my name is Isan Najj Mazar. I'm a PhD candidate in the Chemical Engineering Department and I'm very happy to have this opportunity today to introduce our research. Every year, 9 million tons of plastic end up in the oceans resulting in critical environmental issues. To tackle this problem, there is a high interest in eco-friendly alternatives such as paper-based packaging. However, to make the paper as effective as plastic in terms of properties, it is coding. You certainly use paper cups. It has a special coding that helps keep you doing from leaking. Usually, the most common codings are made from petroleum, like polyethylene, which can make the paper hard to recycle. Since the separation of the coding layer from the paper hinders the recycling of these products. Our study aims to understand the factors that influence the recycling of coded paper. The first step in our research is to develop a lab-based method to evaluate the recyclability of coded paper. Therefore, we looked at existing worldwide recycling standards and methods, which use different equipment and different process conditions. We compared two main recycling equipment in terms of running time, functionality, severity on the fibers, as well as soaking time of the fibers using a special fiber analyzer, which gives us data on fiber properties. Also, fiber recovery was assessed through screenings step. For this aim, both coded and uncoated paper were examined. We found that there is no significant difference between the two equipment. Soaking time does that affect the fiber recovery properties. And finally, with our recommended recycling method, it is possible to evaluate the recyclability of any coded paper. Let's continue to our collective journey towards a greener, cleaner planet for generations to come. Thank you.

transcription: Our next speaker is Limna Suja Shaji. Limna is a materials researcher and passionate science storyteller pursuing her PhD in engineering. She's working on silk biomaterials, sustainable solutions to improve dental care and to change lives. Welcome to the stage Limna for Healing Smiles with Silk a sustainable solution for dental care. I'm sure you know someone who has gone through the pain of losing a tooth or maybe even yourself. It's not just about appearance, it affects how they speak, feel and live each day. Fortunately we have a permanent solution for this problem now. Dental implants which looks and feels like our natural teeth but what if getting an implant means going through multiple surgeries it's even more painful and that's why one in six Australians skipped dental appointments because of anxiety and nearly two-thirds delay them due to cost or even fly overseas for cheaper treatments. So what if I tell you the solution is as simple as a piece of paper like the one you see in the middle of the screen. This is a magic paper made from silk and it has a power to restore smiles. Some is impossible right? Let me explain. When we lose a tooth the bone underneath begins to shrink so it needs to grow back before inserting the implant. To help with this doctors cover the space using special membranes. These are like thin barriers that can protect and guide bone growth. Dental surgeons currently use titanium meshes as membranes. They are safe and effective but there's one problem once the bone growth is complete these meshes has to be removed with the help of another surgery which means more pain more cost and more recovery time for the patient. So what if we had a natural material that slowly breaks down by itself and disappears into the body and there's no need for another surgery. That's where the magic silk paper comes in. In my PhD I'm turning ordinary silk fibers. Yes the same silk you might see in your favorite ties and pajamas into a paper that can support bone growth. In the first space of my research I developed a method to make the paper by cutting and blending the fibers in water creating a smooth battle like mixture called a suspension. This suspension can be layered on plates and dried to form a flexible paper but it's not as simple as it sounds. After plenty of testing and fine tuning I finally made strong papers and here's the best part. Human cells actually grown them which means they are safe and health the body heal opening the dough for some real medical use. Now my next step is to connect with clinicians to support animal testing so we can take them from lab to clinics. With my stilt papers we could cut implant caused by 30% eliminate those extra surgeries and have safer treatments close by but this is just one application. The magic silk paper could transform many other areas of medicine so I'm not just restoring smiles and unfolding a future full of wonderful possibilities. Thank you.

transcription: Kevin Gavallis. Kevin is an analytical chemist. He's using his chemistry expertise to uncover why long-life chocolate milk changes flavor over time, helping tackle a problem that affects food quality and access in rural Australia. Put your hands together for Kevin Gavallis, the flavor of chocolate milk. I'd like to ask you all a question. Have you ever been eating something that you didn't like the taste of? Somebody told you to just block your nose. Did you try it? If you did, what you might have noticed is that the flavor did change, but it was still there. This is a very simple experiment that tells us how important the smell of a food is in determining how it tastes. But now you might be wondering where does smell come from? It's caused by special odor compounds that are present in everything, and these odor compounds can come from a wide range of places, depending on the specific food that we're talking about. In milk, they can come from the grass, the cows are eating, or the water that they drink, or whether they were feeling a little bit stressed. We then make it more complicated by heating the milk up to make it safe to drink. And when we add heat, some of the proteins and the sugars start interacting with each other, giving us even more odor compounds to think about. But in general, we talk about milk being quite plain, and so we add flavorings to make it a little bit interesting. The most popular in the world being, chocolate. But there's a problem. In long life chocolate milk, that rich, delicious chocolate flavor just disappears after 28 days. And nobody knows where it's gone. My journey in finding the chocolate milk, chocolate flavoring, began in 2017, when I immigrated from South Africa to Waga Waga, a rural town in New South Wales. There I spent six years living with, learning from, and working alongside dairy farmers. And I saw how important milk is, not just as a food, but as the lifeblood of thousands of rural Australians. And so for my PhD, I set out to tackle this important problem that is so relevant for so many Australians. I'll be doing this using three studies. In my first study, I'm going to use some advanced chemistry techniques to take apart the milk, allowing me to identify all of those odor compounds, and how important they are to the flavor. Then I'm just going to pop my milk in the cupboard for six months, testing it regularly to see how the odor and the flavor have actually changed. I'm going to take all of this information and working directly with an industry partner, remake the chocolate milk, aiming for a longer-lasting, punchier flavor. So at the end of my PhD, I will come up with a method for scientists to identify bad flavors and fix them so that no matter where you are, be it South Africa or rural Australia, and no matter how long it's been, you can expect a premium flavor to accompany the premium nutrition of your milk products. Thank you.

Suddenly, typical of Victorian weather, there is a huge storm in the rush, Tony falls and injures himself. The rescue team can't get to him because of the rising flood water. In comes in our drones. Drones are cheap, easy to use and a large group of them can work well together to solve complex problems. If you didn't know already, the new South Wales Fire and Rescue team now use drones in difficult rescue operations. But while the single drones that they use may be able to carry smaller objects, my research focuss on how a large group of drones can solve difficult problems. For example, carrying all these food and medicine for Tony and his friends and even that special treat for Benji. If you have used drones before, you know that they can be extremely fragile. While going in the wind and the rain, a moat can get burned and we call this a fault event. When a fault event occurs, it can disturb the drone causing all this to come crashing down. How do you stop this? This is what I will tell you. Let's say you're carrying a tree of drinks in both your hands. Suddenly, you're right hand cramps and you let go. Now, your left hand must flex harder to restore that force that your right hand was providing. Restore. When a fault event occurs, the drone must automatically estimate the power loss and restore that force so that there is no disturbance to the load. To solve this autonomously, I am considering all the sense of feedback and developing control algorithms that will allow the drone to estimate the power loss and restore that force. Using my research, I have been able to reduce the disturbance on the load by up to 90 percent compared to existing methods. But let's say you didn't go to gym that week and you can't flex hard enough. Then, ray-configure. The other healthy drones in the formation can reconfigure themselves so that they carry more of the weight while the affected drone takes a break. To do this, I am considering all the forced data to allow the drones to calculate the best position in the formation with respect to the force they can provide. Finally, using these methods, we can resolve the problem and get all that food and medicine to Tony so he and Benji can go hike another day.

He examines how toxic behavior emerges in online games, how gendered expectations, shape interactions, and how researchers and gamers often speak past each other. Houston, take the stage! Hello, I'm Houston, and this is my character from an online multiplayer game called the Aboo 3. Now as you can see the character was a woman, which in conjunction with the anonymous nature of online gaming, let some that I play with to believe I was a woman in person, which is relevant as time time ago, a person I regularly game with, sent me a series of sorted messages and sexual requests. It wasn't until years later that I realized that was sexual harassment. Now not being a woman myself, much of the language used didn't quite affect me, though I did wonder what my experience would have been if those misassumptions about my gender were true. Now I've since had the opportunity to conduct some research in this area, in a systematic review that we conducted on cyberbullying in online gaming, we found that women and gender diverse players are disproportionately affected by sexual harassment while gaming. That many suffer serious harms to their well-being, and some may even disengage from gaming entirely. But above all, we learn that most gamers, simply, do not care. A sense of callousness and helplessness permeates the community as we resign ourselves to the phrase, it is what it is. There are, of course, many reasons for this, but one of the major challenges we face is a disconnect between gamers and researchers. We don't agree on what the problem is. What researchers define as cyberbullying gamers see as harmless banter. Meanwhile, toxic behaviors actually experience by gamers we don't quite capture using valid measurement tools. According to prevention programs that are ineffective, and in some cases entirely unnecessary, my research now aims to bridge this gap between what gamers experience and what researchers define. We are currently looking at commonalities in cyberbullying victim disclosure on online gaming forums. And in doing so, we hope to better identify the kind of harassment that gamers actually face on a day-to-day basis. And ultimately, develop bullying prevention programs that are community grounded, effective, and may be implemented by regulatory bodies and gaming platforms to better protect gamers online. So, that what happened to me so many years ago. And what happens to gamers on a daily basis can happen just a little less. Thank you.

transcription: Haley King. Haley's PhD topic came from her work experience in a hospital and a desire to amplify the voices of workers who rarely feel heard. Welcome to the stage, Haley. Most of you will have been inside a hospital. You will have seen the doctors and the nurses, but I'm wondering if you noticed the person delivering the meal or the one cleaning. These workers are critical to the successful running of our hospitals. And just like you and I, they must complete their mandatory safety training. You know the one, it's delivered via online learning modules on a computer. And I'm an educator in a public hospital and I support the learning of workers in kitchens, laundries and cleaning to do the training. But I was concerned that the training was not effective. The workers were telling me that it was hard to do and it wasn't relevant to the work that they do every day. Did you know that research, on learning, digital skills and training of unskilled workers is from the perspective of managers and education providers. These workers themselves have never been researched for their perspective on safety training. Driven to understand how we can improve safety training for these so-called unskilled workers, I worked in two commercial kitchens and industrial laundry and as a hospital cleaner for six weeks across two health services. First, I worked photo, but first I completed the applicable mandatory safety training. I realised the workers were right about the relevance of training to the role when another worker physically stopped me from collecting a sheet that had dropped from the claws of that sheet folding machine onto the floor. If she had not done that, I would have been hit on the head by the claws of the machine. I was scared. As a worker and a researcher, I was worried about being injured. But I learnt something that day. The mandatory safety training modules alone would not keep me safe. I was learning to be safe through my experiences on the job and from my peers. And something else, these workers are far from unskilled. They have developed important knowledge about workplace safety, but there's a mismatch between their knowledge and experience and the information being provided in safety training. Safety training is currently designed as an organisational box-ticking exercise and the missing piece in the puzzle in keeping workers safe is work art knowledge. But I've got a plan. I have an education manager, a learning designer, and previously known as unskilled workers, ready to work with me to redesign safety training. We are going to make it relevant to the work completed every day. We're going to make it learn the way that workers learn at work. And we're going to make it engaging because we really only have one plan. Keep the workers safe at work.

transcription: Brianna Giles, fueled by an unyielding curiosity and desire to solve challenging problems, she's dedicated to defeating the formidable opponent, Brain Cancer. Put your hands together for Brianna. Pitch this, a silent time bomb, taking away deep inside your brain. You don't feel it, you don't see it, but it's growing. By the time Brain Cancer is discovered, sadly, it is often too late. This disease can steal your memories, your personality, even your ability to speak or move. In fact, only five out of every 100 people diagnosed will survive for more than five years. But of those lucky few, their lives are plagued with constant illness and tumours returning with evangence. So we ask ourselves, why is Brain Cancer so difficult to treat? The problem lies within the brain. A fortress, shielded by dedicated protectors, meet Lenny, one of our gatekeepers, absolutely brilliant at keeping harmful bacteria and viruses from entering the brain. But here's the catch. Lenny also blocks the entry of most life-saving cancer drugs, preventing them from reaching brain tumours. Now I want you to think for a moment. What if there was a way we could sneak past Lenny? What if we could build a kind of Trojan horse, a smart delivery system, capable of unlocking the brain's defenses, locating the tumour and dropping off cancer-keeling drugs exactly where they needed the most? In my PhD, I'm working on something called the Optomer Express. Think of Optimus, a strands of DNA folded into unique shapes just like the Trojan horse here, programmed with a key that recognizes specific padlocks on the surface of the brain. Lenny here will only let through those keys that match those specific padlocks. Once inside the brain, the Optimus zooms straight towards the tumour. Here, the Trojan horse releases its precious cargo of tiny, powerful drug packages. Think of them as microscopic warriors, trying to attack cancer cells and only cancer cells. That silent ticking time bomb becomes diffused, one Optomer Express at a time. So ultimately, this means we can fight brain cancer more precisely with fewer of those nasty side effects that come with today's treatments. So yes, my project is about clever molecules and smart drug delivery. But really, it's about hope. Hope for better treatments and better lives for brain cancer patients and their families. Thank you.

transcription: Sonia Tarek. Sonia is exploring the environmental impacts of textile waste. She lives between two worlds, imagination and investigation. Together, they inspire her to reflect, reimagine, and help shape a more responsible future. Put your hands together for Sonia. We often think that when we throw something away, Wush, it's gone. Out of sight, out of mind. But even something as basic as the cotton that we wear every day has a life and an afterlife that might just surprise you. Let me explain how. Every year, Australia dumps around 1 million tonnes of textile waste that ends up in landfill. It's like throwing away 9,000 gelong cats football jumper every single minute. About 30% of that has caught in. And because it is a natural fiber, we assume it's safe to compost. But today's cotton isn't just pure cotton. It is dyed. Maybe in a colour you might be wearing now. Treated with chemicals, finishes, brighteners and softeners. These treatments help cotton look better and last longer, but they come with hidden risks. They, when disposed of, can poison the soil, contaminate water and can even enter our food chains. It has been observed that dyes slows down the composting process and that different dyes break down at different rates. So I ask myself, if two cotton shirts, one grade and the other blue, break down differently, they are still leaf different effects on the environment, could one colour help a plant thrive and another silently poison the soil, which can relieve what behind. There is no simple way to find out. That is where my PhD comes in. I analyze compost that once held that cotton to find out what chemical residues it leaves behind. Are they safe or are they toxic? To find them, I use a method called non-target analysis. That scans not only just one chemical, but anything and everything in the compost, knowns and unknowns. So far, I have found these three to four suspicious phenolic compounds that are known for their toxicity and ability to harm microbial life. I have tested some traditional methods too, but with over 400 plus dyes and chemical finishes used around in the world with their own chemical structure, we can't estimate visually that would take our lifetime. That is why we need fast and reliable ways to understand what we are adding in our environment. I am using AI tools, advanced databases and compound libraries to develop new analysis method to study and identify these toxic residues faster and more thoroughly. In this way, we can build our own type specific chemical libraries on which new Australian standards compostable textiles will be developed. The first of these standards is already in the development, bringing this way into reality. So next time you pull on your favourite cotton shirt, remember, it has a life, it will have an afterlife, but with my research, I say for afterlife. Thank you.

transcription: Matt is our next speaker. So Matt is coming from the School of Law. He was puzzled by how the government afforded the COVID pandemic spending and he's been on a mission ever since to understand just where does the money come from. Put your hands together for Matt Crocker. Do you remember how the Australian government spent an enormous amount of money during COVID? How overnight the government found $130 billion to spend on JobKeeper? At the time I was halfway through my masters of economics and besides all the other questions I had about COVID I couldn't work out for the life of me how the government had found all this money. How could it be that this government who for the last ten years had been telling us we have to live within our means, how could it be that they had found all this money? I was left asking myself, where does the money come from? Intuitively we all know that the Australian government makes Australian dollars and for anyone else to do so is illegal. But at the same time we had taught that the government needs our taxpayer dollars and that it can only spend as much as it collects and taxes or borrows. Time and time again we hear that they don't have money to pay our nurses more or invest in our public schools. But what I couldn't get passed was the reality that when the government needed to step in as it did during COVID the question about where will the money come from didn't even get a mention. So I asked my economics professors to explain to me how the government's finances work. They talked about budget constraints and showed me fancy equations yet no one I spoke with could explain to me how the government spends and how it finances that spending. And herein lays the problem. The government's accounting structure and how the government actually spends remains poorly explained. But three years ago I embarked on a PhD to change that. My research approach has been to describe the evolution of the laws that set out how governments in Australia have spent. From the arrival of the first fleet in 1788 to the establishment of the Central Bank in 1912 all the way up to how the government's accounts at the RBA operate today. My research has been archival complemented by with interviews with public servants. By meticulously tracing the evolution of the legislative history and with a precise focus on describing the accounting structure I have identified where the government's money comes from. And the truth is the answer was staring at us all along. The government makes the money. It spends before it taxes or borrows. Now my findings are controversial. I get that it flips the narrative on its head. But what we thought constrains the government's capacity to spend is not a constraint at all. For the government finding the money is never the issue. Finding the resources, the labour, the know how that is the challenge. So instead of asking themselves where will the money come from, governments need ask themselves will this spending create inflation? My research has been picked up by the conversation in the ABC. But my hope is that it pushes policymakers, politicians, journalists to debate government spending proposals on their potential to create inflation. But if I can leave you with one thing tonight, the next time you hear somebody say the government can't afford it, remind them that the government makes the money.

transcription: Situated somewhere between criminology, politics and law, Oscars research into truth-telling and transitional justice hopes to ensure that future truth commissions in Australia deliver meaningful outcomes for first Australians, which are hands together for Oscar Key. To start, as we are gathered on Ng, I would like to acknowledge and pay my respects to the war-in-jury peoples. The acknowledgement of country to me is not some empty platitude. The first time I heard one, it took me by surprise. See, I come from Singapore and all I knew about Australia back then was the Wiggles, Steve Irwin and Stingrays. But ever since I've been drawn deeper into understanding Australia's non-colonial history, which has led me to my problem today, Oscar, what's a truth commission? I'm glad you asked. A truth commission is a fact-finding inquiry which seeks to document colonial harms, promote healing and recommend solutions. But that's not the problem. The problem is, they suck. They suck because fundamental understandings of truth and justice are completely different between First Nations philosophies and the predominantly Western philosophies that govern Australia. That in turn leads to an inability or unwillingness for the government to listen to First Australians. That dooms truth commissions to failure from the start. We are 30 years on from two major truth commissions. One, said stops over-incasrating Indigenous Australians. The other said stop stealing Indigenous children from their families. Instead of improving things, we have instead doubled the rate at which we incarcerate First Australians. We have doubled the rate at which we steal Indigenous children from their families. To add to this, a year ago, a commission in Melbourne handed down 46 commission recommendations to the government of which it supported only four. That sucks. For things to get better, we must listen to what First Australians want out of these commissions, what they want to see from the outcomes and procedures, which is where my research comes in. I am interviewing politically active and non-academic Australians to understand what they want out of these truth commissions. I have also interviewed ex-commissioners about what they have done and what they would do differently. Could they do it all over again? Armed with this knowledge, we can ensure that future commissions won't have just four recommendations supported. They would have a majority of recommendations supported. And this affects not just Australia but other countries like Canada and New Zealand as well. Now granted, the impact from this research won't be seen in a year or a decade, but over a generation. No change takes time, but it starts here with listening.

transcription: Hi, I'm Jacinda, this is Nick and we are APARO. We are automating insurance billing for medical practices. We are a team with deep expertise in health care and software. Nick was an engineer at Apple and the NSA. I was the CTO and and founding engineer at Doctor on Demand, which raised over 160 million in venture capital. At Doctor on Demand, we submitted millions of claims to insurance and I saw first hand in industry full of siloed systems and manual processes. So manual that the New York Times reported that there are still seven billing staff employed for every ten doctors that is insanely inefficient and is why the US spends more than $330 billion every single year just processing payments. At APARO, we solved this for medical practices by providing automated claim submission, integrated online patient billing and for newer practices, modern APIs. Practices love us because we give them one unified system for all their payments. Previously, they were manually reconciling multiple disparate systems. We only launched two months ago and already have clients with an aggregate tens of millions in revenue of which our take is 5%. We are APARO. We are automating insurance and patient billing in one unified payments platform, have an expert team and already have clients and are rapidly adding more. We would love to talk with you. Thank you.
